Copper Scroll · entries 20–23 · 28 September 2026

Qumran: what the footage resolves

The aerial sequence supplies gorge context and a probable cave match. Archival photographs identify a tunnel mouth more securely. The upstream intake, boulder and wall remain unconnected in the reviewed views.

Result: retain the existing candidate order and low exact-feature confidence. None of these images identifies a Copper Scroll hiding place.

Solid cyan: visible outline · dashed amber: probable identity

Comparison with the two published plans

Each redrawing retains its own source coordinate system. Perspective views above are not registered to these plans.

Ilan–Amit, Fig. 1

1989, p. 283. A: visible intake, point 3. C: branch / short tunnel. D: long tunnel. The dashed basin-edge dam is a reconstruction.

Reeder–Jol, Fig. 4

2006, p. 229; survey in 2002. B: large rock below the pothole. The reported upstream wall is distinct from Ilan’s hypothetical main-wadi dam.

What this leaves open

Under a whole-conduit reading of entry 21, A remains the first feature to investigate. A branch-head reading gives C more weight. A northward approach to Sekakah requires a different test from a rock north of a channel. The sampled images settle none of these alternatives.

For entry 22, the generally eastern position of the long tunnel relative to Ilan’s basin is only a conditional fit: the reservoir’s name and the individual fissure remain unidentified. Entry 20 retains the heap/dam dispute; entry 23 still lacks secure distance endpoints.

Manual outlines are image annotations, with unknown ground accuracy. The 01:38 marks follow visible edges only; concealed basin limits are omitted. Video inspected at 5-second intervals and at 1-second intervals from 01:15–01:45, plus selected full-size frames. Two watermarked stills are used here for source criticism. Capture date, camera calibration and coordinates are unknown.
